entry.summary:

Source: @jalaeipour

"He was so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness."

In his autobiography, the late Arthur Arberry writes of the late Reynold A. Nicholson — scholar, commentator, and translator of literary and mystical works from Persian and Arabic into English:

He was a consummate scholar, so enamored of his books that he sacrificed his eyesight to ceaseless reading, so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness. In the final years of his life, when the lamp of his eyes was flickering toward extinction, he composed this verse — a poem that, to me, among all the last words ever uttered by human beings, carries the truest inspiration and the most moving farewell:

When Truth appears unveiled before your eyes,
These tongues are left bewildered and surprised.
*I shall fall silent — the Beloved has come to speak:*
*Listen, and God knows best what is right and true.*
*Become devoid of sense, of hearing, and of thought,*
*That you may hear the summons "Return!"*
As long as this tongue remains, you shall not hear the Word.
So words must be brief. And peace.

**I have borrowed the Persian rendering of Nicholson's poem from verses of the Masnavi. The asterisked lines are from the Masnavi.

- Nicholson's poem, as narrated by Arberry, reads:
When Truth shines out words fail and nothing tell;
Now hear the Voice within your hearts. Farewell.

This is the closing verse of a long poem that Arberry quoted and confirmed earlier in this same piece, noting that in these verses Nicholson was deeply influenced by Rumi: ... He seldom spoke of his personal beliefs, and I, too, in twenty-five years of close friendship with him, learned little about how he was raised or of his spiritual journey. Yet the image that took shape in my mind was that he, like many others, had lost his faith in youth and then recovered it through intellectual companionship and kinship of spirit with Muslim mystics.

In his old age, he composed a poem in which, for the first time, he laid bare his innermost thoughts. It was clear that these thoughts had been profoundly shaped by long years of studying Rumi's works ...

Mohammad Mehdi Mojahedi

Source: @jalaeipour

Thomas Schelling, the Nobel laureate in economics, once wrote that violence can be the continuation of diplomacy by other means — a proposition that today applies to Iran-US relations more than ever. So much so that negotiations between the two countries are unfolding not in an atmosphere of trust, but under the shadow of war and threats, where force is not the opposite of diplomacy but has become part of its very logic. In this framework, Trump's approach to negotiation rests more on applying pressure and setting deadlines than on pursuing a win-win agreement. For him, negotiation is less a process for the gradual convergence of the parties and more a tool for dictating terms. Consequently, any sign of a tactical approach to negotiation aimed at buying time is read as stalling and can push the other side toward resorting to force. Indeed, the rationale behind the twelve-day war can be understood through this same logic. For America, that war was not an interruption of diplomacy but the driving force behind another round of negotiations. Now Washington, drawing on the battlefield and psychological outcomes of the war, has entered negotiations from a position it finds desirable — one in which red lines have been drawn by force and negotiation is merely about how to consolidate them. Under such circumstances, Iran does not face a simple choice. Accepting negotiation under the shadow of war can be construed as accepting the logic of pressure, while rejecting it carries the risk of heightened confrontation. What matters more than this binary is understanding how the nature of negotiation has changed: an agreement in such an atmosphere is not the product of confidence-building but the outcome of a perceived balance of power. On this basis, the ultimate question about the outcome of the negotiations is the very question Schelling raised: can the threat be contained and kept in the service of diplomacy, or has the logic of ultimatum and war reduced negotiation to a ceremonial affair? The answer to this question will determine the fate of Iran-US negotiations and the future of the region.@katechon6

In the second half of the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

New micro-schools: mosque-schools and home-schools

In the second half of the 1990s, some households, arguing that schools were not religious enough, pulled their children out of school and created a form of home-schooling. The COVID-19 outbreak further entrenched this arrangement, albeit on a very limited scale. Out of this current, mosque-schools gradually took shape; first established in Qom, they multiplied rapidly and today have branches in 22 provinces, overseen by a central headquarters. Over the past 4 years, the number of these schools has more than doubled to over 450, with an average of roughly 30 students per school. After several years of operation, these schools were finally granted operating licenses starting in 1402 as a type of non-governmental school, and they also signed agreements with the government to expand into rural areas. Because these schools use mosque facilities, their tuition is lower, and beyond more extensive religious instruction, they also offer skills training and income-generation programs—particularly income generation through cyberspace and cryptocurrencies.

Alongside this current, a trend of establishing home-schools has also emerged, starting in Tehran and growing rapidly. These too are schools with a student body of between 20 and 40, charging very high tuition, and are often run with supplementary curricula in more private settings. Many of these home-schools are in practice smaller branches of, or affiliated with, a private school. Despite the Ministry of Education's current opposition, these schools do not conflict with the ministry's overall policy logic and face no obstacle to expansion. Home-schools are in the early stages of becoming established, and their activities have so far been reported in some areas of Tehran as well as the metropolises of Tabriz and Isfahan.

The spread of these micro-schools signals the continuation and intensification of differentiation and the ever-increasing stratification of parts of society into smaller units—a kind of intra-group and intra-class fragmentation. Mosque-schools represent a form of differentiation among more religious families themselves, just as home-schools represent further differentiation among the upper strata of society. These schools should not be conflated with diversity in the educational system, because educational diversity is positive only when it is accompanied by universal access and the possibility of genuine choice for all social groups. Although these schools currently account for a negligible share of the educational system, they are significant in terms of institutional analysis.@Omidi_Reza

Today's Iranian media have headlined this sentence from the President's speech at the annual summit of the "West Asia Union": This year, for the first time in West Asia, extreme poverty was eradicated, and we have no hungry, homeless, out-of-school, or treatment-deprived people. I remember all the years we longed to read such a headline. I remember all the elections in which we pushed to make the eradication of extreme poverty a slogan and a priority for the candidates, and twice it happened, but sanctions, war, and misgovernance prevented its full realization. The deep smile of satisfaction that reading this headline has brought to my lips—I cannot hide it on the metro. The unknown old man across from me, wearing a beautiful Kurdish outfit, smiles too upon seeing my smile. We are immersed in the sweetness of our smiles when my daughter calls from Lark, and her image appears on my smart glasses. Simultaneously with the West Asia Union summit, the Hormuz Festival has been held on the islands of Hormuz, Hengam, and Lark. For several years now, it has brought together the best musicians and the most beautiful clothing and artistic rituals of the residents around the Persian Gulf and thousands of participants from across Iran and the Persian Gulf and other countries, and it has become the most popular art festival of the Global South. The presence of any smart robot at the festival is not permitted, and this very rule has made the ecomuseums of these islands more attractive to young people. My daughter, along with two of her classmates, has gone to participate in the festival by electric high-speed train to Bandar Abbas and from there by electric ship to Lark. She is excited about the beauty of the beaches and the art of the participants and the joy of socializing with friends she discovered at this same festival last year. In a three-dimensional video call from Lark, as last year, she insists that we not stay in Tehran and migrate to Hengam Island. Enthusiastically, she recounts that at iftar in the Shahid Tangsiri Mosque of Lark, shrimp do-piazeh and halva were hosted by the locals. She says: "Dad, just let go of Tehran already! Isn't it a shame to miss even a single day of walking along the shore to watch the sunrise or sunset or the moon?" As it happens, her mother and I have had this same wish for years, and since the beginning of our acquaintance and love, our most beautiful memories and experiences have been tied to the islands around Qeshm and the coasts of Hormozgan, but since the time of Corona and then the wars of 1404 and 1405 and the eventful years after, we were forced to stay and help in Tehran. Now that we see our Iran has flourished and for several years has remained the connecting ring of the world, green and safe, and Samaneh's design and my party work and attendance in the girl's classes at Shahid Minab High School can all be followed in cyberspace, perhaps the time has come to act on her suggestion. entry.summary:

Source: @jalaeipour

Gentlemen in charge! A society that has been economically squeezed by war, sanctions, and siege becomes more sensitive, more on edge, and more vulnerable. The smallest social conflict in such an atmosphere carries a far higher cost than under normal conditions. A family grappling with inflation, job insecurity, anxiety over medicine, housing, and their children's future has far less capacity to endure new tensions. At this point, the quality of social policy is directly tied to the country's capacity to pull through the crisis. Every policy must be measured against a simple question: Does this policy, at this moment, strengthen social bonds or further inflame existing fractures? Provocative identity debates, cultural disputes such as hijab, the proposal to lash a female singer, the widespread criminalization of social behaviors, actions that set parts of society against other parts, and the reopening of cases such as how women dress are not merely a cultural or legal matter. Under crisis conditions, these policies carry a secondary consequence as well: they divert part of society's political, disciplinary, and psychological energy away from the main problem and activate divisions that you must accept Iranian society has moved past and that the people must be respected for — yet under economic pressure, these divisions have the potential to become a social fracture. In this sense, a country in crisis needs something akin to a "social ceasefire" — meaning preventing the creation of conflicts that are not urgent and that can drain the country's limited social capital.

One. The owner of himself always grieves and melts. We became…

Saadi Pharmacy

One.
The owner of himself always grieves and melts.
We became the owner of a full-bodied kingdom and were freed.
(Saadi)
When we consider ourselves our own owner, we melt from grief. When we consider the kingdom and the owned to belong to that beautiful Unique One, we become free and liberated. "Inna lillah" means we belong to Him. We are not our own owners.

▫️Two.
Every foot that entered the house found a treasure;
No longer would all its life be at the market.
(Saadi)
There is a treasure that is found in the realm of the heart. One who finds the way to the inner treasure is freed from dependence on markets. Bayazid Bastami said about the meaning of dervishhood: "The one who, in the corner of his own heart, finds a foot entering a treasure..."

▫️Three.
One who became a stranger to wealth and greatness and lordship,
Is familiar to whomever he reaches.
(Saadi)
One who sees himself free from names and positions and passing powers can be familiar and close to everyone. If we are captivated by our own greatness and lordship and wealth, if we are bound by our position and name and reputation and intelligence and knowledge, we lose the felicity of "familiarity."

▫️Four.
Whoever does not know gratitude for today's blessing
Will eat regret upon the portion of tomorrow's mercy.
(Saadi)
One who does not appreciate the gifts of this world and does not welcome them with gratitude and joy will also be deprived of the mercy of the next world.

Whoever does not see today in the world the countenance of the Friend,
It is most likely that tomorrow he will have no vision.
(Saadi)
The beauty of nature and the movement and growth of the earth is a mercy of this world:
"Fa-unzur ila athar rahmatillah kayfa yuhyi al-arda ba'da mawtiha" (Surah Rum, verse 50)
"Look at these signs of Allah's kindness, how He revives the earth after its death." (Translation of Tafsir Kashf al-Asrar)

▫️Five.
Except the remembrance of the Friend, whatever you do is wasted life;
Except the secret of love, whatever you say is vanity.
(Saadi)
If life is not mixed with the remembrance of the Friend, and is not spent in longing for the Friend, it is wasted. It has passed in vanity:
Saadi, if he does not risk love, what shall he do with the kingdom of existence?
It is a pity that a whole life should go to waste.

The remembrance and recollection of the Friend has no end. It is not tiresome either. Because it is the food of the soul. The bread and water of the soul:
Our speech grew long and still remains,
For the remembrance of the Friend brings no weariness whatsoever.
(Saadi)
Therefore, his regret is for the times that passed unaware of the Friend:
Whatever we said other than the tale of the Friend,
In all our life we regret it.
(Saadi)
If there is any regret, it is nothing but this: why did we not breathe in His remembrance more? Why did we not throb in longing for Him more?
So that precious life does not end in regret,
All night Your remembrance was ongoing and repeated.

Speaking with Him, speaking of Him, and floating in the "tale of the Friend" is the meaning of life.

〰 Seddiq Qotbi

🎒 Economic sanctions and the educational future of children

There was a time when economic sanctions were presented as an alternative to war, and many hoped this approach could resolve international disputes without war and destruction, while others dismissed it as ineffective. But as time passed, these assumptions were met with fundamental doubts. It gradually became clear that economic sanctions leave irreversible damage in people's lives.

Mohammad Javad Dashti-Manesh, an economic researcher, examines in this piece one of the studies conducted on the intergenerational effects of sanctions on the educational future of Iranian children, emphasizing that economic pressures must not be allowed to narrow children's educational opportunities and growth.

The findings of this study show that the long-term damage of sanctions manifests in ways such as the cancellation of remedial and supplementary classes, and even dropping out of school, and in the years to come, it will impose itself in the form of limited job and income opportunities on the generation that sits behind school desks today.
